extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, and law students drafting or litigating patent specifications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for what a patent specification must contain and how it must be drafted so as to be valid and not misleading; includes examples and case-law illustrating sufficiency, ambiguity, drawings, and disclosure obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of necessary matter is fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission to mention in the specification anything which the patentee knows to be necessary for the beneficial enjoyment of his invention, is a fatal defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: Neilson v. Harford (317, 321). If a particular temperature or other essential condition is not stated and experiments are necessary to achieve benefit, the patent is void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of merely contributory matters not fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission to mention something which contributes only to the degree of the benefit is not fatal provided the apparatus described would work beneficially and be worth adopting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: omission of water twyres not invalid where beneficial effect can be produced without them and their use is within ordinary knowledge (Neilson v. Harford 318).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification need not repeat what's in ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not describe that which is within the knowledge of any workman who would be employed to put up the apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: condenser in gas apparatus (Crossley v. Beverley). Ordinary mechanics' knowledge may be assumed; however, material old parts applied in a new way must be described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee must disclose best known means at enrolment
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is bound to insert in his specification the most improved means of carrying out his invention with which he is acquainted at the time of the enrolment of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If improvements made during the allowed time for the specification exist, they should be described; otherwise objection may arise (cases cited at lb. 116–117).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe improvements discovered before enrolment
rubrics_metrics.description: All improvements made during the interval for enrolling the specification should be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: otherwise the patentee might unfairly prolong monopoly by later patenting mere contrivances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresenting importance vitiates specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The insertion or representation of anything as important, not being so in fact, will vitiate the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Huddart v. Grimshaw. Introducing things as essential when they are not may indicate intent to mislead the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous or misleading directions void patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent are void if the specification be ambiguous, or give directions which tend to mislead the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Turner v. Winter. Using a generic term when only one species works (e.g., 'fossil salt' vs 'sal gem') can invalidate the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a named class contains unusable members it's bad
rubrics_metrics.description: If a whole class of substances is stated as suitable and any one of them will not answer the purpose, the specification is bad as misleading the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bickford v. Skewes (218). Leave the public no ground to choose a member of a class that won't work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must state method to remove injurious foreign matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If a substance as generally known contains foreign matter which is positively injurious, the plaintiff must show that a method of easily removing such foreign matter is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derosne v. Farie (157) — if removal is necessary to make the substance efficacious, the specification must address it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance named must answer the proposed purpose beneficially
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance named in the specification must answer the purpose proposed beneficially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the described substance cannot produce the intended effect for the asserted uses, the specification is insufficient (Derosne v. Farie 163–164).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must state at least one method that will succeed
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification must state at least one method which will succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no workable method is disclosed, the patent is invalid (case law cited at lb. 165).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need not list every possible substitutable substance
rubrics_metrics.description: All the substances which will answer the purpose of the invention need not be stated, only the public must not be misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: permissible breadth, but avoid claiming a class when not all members are suitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must disclose the plainest and easiest method
rubrics_metrics.description: The plainest and most easy way of production must be stated; if obscure terms are employed to induce belief that elaborate processes are necessary when simple ones will succeed, the specification is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Savory v. Price (83). The patentee should point out the simplest mode he uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot claim a false 'preference' to mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee states that he prefers a certain material, having ascertained that no other would answer, he misleads the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crompton v. Ibbotson (83) — don't assert exclusivity of a preferred material unless true.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a named article is not procurable under that name, must be identified
rubrics_metrics.description: If an article is described by a particular name which is not ordinarily used or it cannot be procured under that name, the specification must state where it may be procured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sturtz v. De La Rue (83) — absence of procurement information can render disclosure insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studied or manifest ambiguity will vitiate
rubrics_metrics.description: A studied or manifest ambiguity in the specification will vitiate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Galloway v. Bleaden (524). Courts scrutinize suspected deliberate ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/scientific terms acceptable if target audience can understand
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no objection prima facie that a specification contains terms of art requiring explanation; scientific terms not understood by ordinary persons are fine if intelligible to scientific persons, but common language that misleads ordinary persons is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neilson v. Harford (341) — explain technical meanings if they differ from common usage (e.g., 'malt' meaning prepared barley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement must be clearly presented as such
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention is an improvement, it must distinctly appear on the face of the specification as such, and not as an original discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hill v. Thompson (247). The specification must inform the public what is new and what is old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must teach the invention and warn of prohibited use
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is to warn the public of what is prohibited, and to teach them the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morgan v. Seaward (173) and MacFarland v. Price (74) — be explicit about the scope of prohibition and instruction for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistakes not necessarily fatal if non-misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: A mistake in a specification does not of necessity vitiate the patent where it is foreign to the invention and cannot mislead; inaccurate use of words explained by context will not vitiate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neilson v. Harford (340, 353, 369) — materiality and potential to mislead govern effect of errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of description is a jury question
rubrics_metrics.description: The sufficiency of the specification in matters of description is a question for the jury; the jury's finding on distinctness is conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Walton v. Potter (595); Bickford v. Skewes (219–220) — factual issue for trier of fact whether public would be misled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff must clearly state objections
rubrics_metrics.description: The attention of the plaintiff must be fully and clearly directed to the objection to the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to frame and direct precise objections can affect proceedings (Bickford v. Skewes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common defects summary (eight defects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification is bad when: 1) terms are ambiguous; 2) necessary descriptions omitted; 3) parts claimed are not original; 4) things are put in to mislead; 5) the drawings are incorrect; 6) one of different ways/ingredients named fails; 7) one of several effects specified is not produced; 8) the things described are not the best known to the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a concise checklist of recurring defects in English law (note from Godson's work). Use as screening rubric for adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: New parts must be accurately described as to operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every part of the invention which is new must be accurately described, as to the manner in which it is to operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Felton v. Greaves — e.g., if a machine requires one roller rough and one smooth for a particular article (scissors), the specification must disclose that configuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describing the same subject as 'whole' acceptable for improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification describing a machine as a whole is sufficient, though the invention be an improvement on a former patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmon v. Playne (75) — but the new elements should still be pointed out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic 'other materials' language does not save insufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The insertion of words like 'other materials may be used' or 'any other substance' does not cure lack of disclosure; such generality may be nearly fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clegg / cases: if the specification speaks mainly of coal (not oil) then 'other substances' must be read in light of what practical men then considered usable; cannot be stretched to all combustible matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: If several results specified and one is old, patent may be void
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be several things specified that may be produced, and one of them is not new, the whole patent is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brunton v. Hawkes — specifying multiple outcomes where one is old may invalidate the entire grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introducing useless or unused parts suggests concealment
rubrics_metrics.description: If things useless and unnecessary have been mixed with a substance, or attached to a machine (especially parts never used by the patentee), the patent is void as they indicate an attempt to overload and mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Arkwright's machine — parts never used were seen as intended to mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large unnecessary parts presumed intended to perplex
rubrics_metrics.description: If any considerable part of a manufacture be unnecessary to produce the desired effect, it will be presumed that it was inserted only with a view to perplex and embarrass the inquirer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner v. Winter and Savory v. Price illustrate this presumption; the patentee must rebut it by showing bona fide use or reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Previously used parts later abandoned acceptable with reason
rubrics_metrics.description: If unnecessary parts had been once fairly introduced and not laid aside until discovered unnecessary later, the patentee may cease to use them without prejudice provided a good reason is given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumption is against inventor until he gives a good reason for discontinuance; Watts example where items not claimed as part of subject did not harm intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings/models: annex when necessary to describe subject
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absolutely necessary to annex to the specification a model, diagram, picture, or drawing descriptive of the manufacture; if without it the subject is clearly described it may be omitted, otherwise drawings are generally adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically scales and full proportions were required (Arkwright). Modern rule: if a common mechanic can make it from perspective drawing, scale may be unnecessary; drawings may supplement words and together enable construction (Bloxam v. Elsee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words and drawings may be read together
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor is allowed to call in aid the drawings annexed to the specification; if by comparison of the words and the drawings the one explains the other sufficiently to enable a skilful mechanic to perform the work, such a specification is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if some names or language in drawings are foreign, relative proportions can suffice; the writing need not alone contain all dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must be adapted to the end; avoid speculative multiple methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The means must be adapted to the end: the description must not give several ways and methods which may or may not answer according to the skill exercised; such multiplicity can mislead the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winter's patent and Turner v. Winter examples — listing many salts or many methods without pointing to the successful one misleads readers and is grounds for invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish new from old; don't present old as novel
rubrics_metrics.description: If any parts are described as essential without a protest against any novelty being attached to them, it will seem though they are old that they are claimed as new; construction will be against patentee seeking to monopolize more than invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: describe whole subject, then explicitly point out parts which are old and well known so as not to mislead (Campion v. Benyon, and related discussion).
